title: Samsung 990 PRO 2TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe M.2 SSD $524.80 Delivered @ Amazon UK via AU
body:
Deal: Samsung 990 PRO 2TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe M.2 SSD $524.80 Delivered @ Amazon UK via AU

[Ishy] I fell like this is a bit to pricey compared to this deal not to long ago IMO
https://www.ozbargain.com.au/node/968847
[onyx981] Temporarily. Companies are already cancelling their subscriptions to bigger ai providers responsible for hoarding hardware because cheaper alternatives exist that run on lower power hardware.
[KangaDrew] Technically true, but it’s mostly workload segmentation, not companies abandoning frontier providers. They’re using cheaper models for routine stuff and keeping the more expensive ones for complex work. But there’s no clear evidence of cancellations en masse.
And changing the direction slightly by adopting a multi-model strategy doesn’t mean SSD and RAM prices will ease soon. AI and data-centre demand is still soaking up supply, so we’ve likely got at least another year or two of pain coming down the pipe.
[onyx981] @KangaDrew: Depends. Chinese models are 'good enough' and are able to do the similar work with a fraction of the gpu, ram and storage requirements. People expect frontier models to be reserved for just enterprise niches and research eventually, depends how long we take to get there. The 1-2 year estimate people have been throwing around may be a lot sooner. The last 3 months alone were wild with the amount of consistent breakthroughs coming out of China with optimisations like Dpark reducing latency by 90% in many cases and making training 6x faster proving frontier models are really operating on unoptimised glut trying to fix their scaling issues with more hardware which may eventually become useless sooner than they expected
[KangaDrew] @onyx981: Yeah, Chinese models and new optimisation techniques are quickly changing the entire landscape. But that doesn’t automatically reduce overall hardware demand. DSpark improves throughput, sure, but not training speed. That just makes existing hardware work harder, but it doesn’t remove the need for it.
Cheaper models will likely take over much of the routine work from the frontier ones, but those lower costs can just as easily have a rebound effect and drive far more usage. That means AI demand and pressure on chip pricing are unlikely to ease any time soon.
